input: "You can have the hour without giving me the letter." I take another chair, leaving his page out of my sight. I arrange some tea for us and settle with my own writing. "Would quiet company help, or would you rather talk about something that has nothing to do with your family's plans?" I leave it to him, and don't read over his shoulder.
output:
The brass kettle on the sideboard ticks itself toward a boil. Rashid watches you take the chair opposite rather than beside him, and watches you turn your attention deliberately to your own page.

“Quiet first,” he says. “Talking later, perhaps.”

He accepts a cup of tea with a brief nod. The letter stays beneath his forearm, its contents hidden, but after a while he takes up his pen.

The room settles around its separate occupations. Thessaly firms dark soil around the rosemary cutting with two careful fingers. Seraphel works salve into the base of a stubborn feather, occasionally making a small, offended sound when it catches. Firelight pulls red from the carved Garvey faces above the mantel.

Your pen scratches. Rashid’s does not.

At last he exhales through his nose. “My sister’s first letter asked whether the Academy library contains forbidden books, whether dragons sleep on gold, and whether demons set things alight when offended.”

From her chair, Seraphel looks up.

“Tell her the shelves are tall and dust is deep;  
The dragons read, the demons rarely sleep.”

Rashid’s mouth twitches. “That is almost useful.”

“It is entirely true,” Thessaly says, without looking up.

He glances toward the doors, where Ashara has not appeared, then back to the page. “My sister is eleven. She can identify evasion at fifty paces, particularly from me.” His fingers tap once against the sealed blankness of the paper. “You said you write letters sometimes.”

He shifts the sheet a fraction farther under his hand, protecting it even as he asks.

“Do you know how to write to someone so they believe you thought of them before the postal schedule compelled you?”
